opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it becomes more and more important as tasks get longer. When you have a short task, maybe five or ten tool calls, a dead end in the context doesn't hurt much. The model sees it tried something, it didn't work, and it moves on. That's actually useful information.

But on really long-horizon tasks, where you're running hundreds of steps, those failed attempts pile up. They take up space, and they also pull the model's attention back toward things that didn't work. Sometimes the model even fixates on an earlier wrong idea because it's sitting right there in the context. So there's a real cost to keeping everything.

The way I think about it is similar to how a person works. If I'm debugging something for a whole day, I don't hold every wrong hypothesis in my head in full detail. I remember, "I tried X, it didn't work because of Y," and I compress that into a short lesson. I think agents need to do the same. Instead of keeping the full transcript of a bad path, you'd like to collapse it into a short note, something like "approach A failed because the API doesn't support this," and drop the raw logs.

There are a few ways to do that. You can have the model summarize or compact its own context periodically. You can give it a scratchpad or memory file where it writes down what it's learned, so you can be more aggressive about clearing the history. Or you can use sub-agents: send a sub-agent off to explore something, and only the result comes back to the main agent, not all the messy exploration.

The tricky part is knowing what's actually a bad path. Sometimes something looks like a dead end and later turns out to matter. So I'm cautious about pruning too aggressively. You want to keep the lesson even if you throw away the details. But overall, I think context management, including cleaning out failed attempts, is going to be one of the key skills that separates agents that can work for hours from ones that fall apart after twenty minutes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated problems right now. When tasks were five or ten tool calls long, context management basically didn't matter. You could just keep appending everything and the model would sort it out. But once you're talking about agents running for hours, doing hundreds of steps, the context becomes this archaeological record of every dead end you went down, and that's actively harmful, not just wasteful.

The thing people underestimate is that a bad path isn't neutral. If the model spent twenty steps trying an approach that didn't work, those twenty steps are still sitting there, and they pull on the model's attention. It'll keep half-believing assumptions it already disproved, or it'll get anchored on a file it looked at that turned out to be irrelevant. So pruning isn't just about fitting in the window, it's about keeping the model's picture of the world accurate.

What we've found works is being pretty aggressive about summarization at natural boundaries. When the agent finishes a sub-task or abandons an approach, you want to collapse that whole episode into something like "tried X, didn't work because Y, moved on." You keep the lesson and throw away the transcript. The failure mode to watch for is over-pruning, where you lose the one detail that mattered, so you want the model itself deciding what's worth keeping, rather than some fixed heuristic.

Longer term I think a lot of this gets pushed into the model. Models are getting better at ignoring stale context and at writing good notes to themselves. But right now, if you're building long-running agents, you should be thinking about context as something you actively curate, not something that just accumulates.

astra-6.text:
I think it becomes more important as tasks get longer, because the context contains not just what the agent has learned, but also all the things it tried that didn’t work. Those failed attempts can keep influencing what it does next.

The tricky part is that you don’t want to forget the lesson. If you tried an approach and discovered it couldn’t work, you want to preserve that conclusion and the reason, without necessarily keeping every intermediate step. Otherwise, the agent may just repeat the same mistake.

So I think you want context management that retains the goal, the current state, and the useful evidence, while compressing the exploration that got you there. The context should increasingly look like a useful handoff to someone picking up the task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it becomes more important the longer the task runs. An agent tries something, it doesn’t work, and now all of that is sitting in its context. If you keep every failed attempt, the model has to keep figuring out which information is still relevant and which conclusions have already been invalidated.

But you don’t want to throw away the lesson from the failure. You want to preserve, “We tried this approach, it failed for this reason,” without preserving every intermediate step. So the useful distinction is between the history of the work and the state of the work: what we’re trying to accomplish, what we know, what we’ve ruled out, and what we should do next.

As tasks get longer, managing that state becomes a bigger part of making the agent reliable.
